title: Gravity Dash
headline: Movement built for floors, walls, and ceilings.
premise: A gravity-changing runner with connected race courses, Lucky Block power-ups, a currency shop, and collectible cosmetics.
proof: Custom movement, generated courses, and the features around the race.

play.title: Run across walls, then make the character your own
play.description: Race through connected rooms as gravity changes, grabbing power-ups from Lucky Blocks, from homing projectiles to thrown bombs. Away from the course, spend in-game currency on rotating crates and manage collected cosmetics.

explode.title: How changing gravity affects the game
explode.description: The game checks nearby surfaces, decides which way is down, and updates movement and animation. Connected course rooms share a common way to measure progress.

layers.title: 01 / Check nearby surfaces
layers.detail: Combine the directions of nearby surfaces to determine gravity.

layers.title: 02 / Update the character
layers.detail: Use that gravity direction for movement, orientation, and animation.

layers.title: 03 / Connect the course
layers.detail: Align room entrances and exits, then record progress along the route.

cases.title: Movement and animation on different surfaces
cases.player: The character’s movement and animations follow its changing sense of down.
cases.technical: The controller consumes combined surface normals and drives a custom VectorForce / BodyGyro rig. StateTracker projects velocity onto the current gravity axis to distinguish running, jumping, and free fall. Exclusion tags keep solid containment geometry from accidentally redirecting gravity; round boundaries explicitly reset the controller.
cases.tradeoff: Surface sampling is adapted and credited. The contribution presented here is controller integration, coordinate-state handling, resets, and edge-case engineering. Continuous floor-to-wall-to-ceiling behavior still needs a current capture.

cases.title: Building connected race courses
cases.player: Room layouts connect to form courses with changes in direction and elevation.
cases.technical: Entrance and Exit transforms align consecutive room templates. StartArc, RoomLength, and CheckpointArc let progress, checkpoints, and culling share a monotonic arc coordinate. An occupancy guard prevents culling a room containing a living player. seedFromExisting can reconstruct an unordered room chain through greedy position/orientation matching.
cases.tradeoff: Chain reconstruction is source-verified; a particular operational purpose such as server restart recovery is not established. No generation speed or performance benchmark is claimed.

cases.title: Homing shots and thrown bombs
cases.player: Homing shots curve toward a locked target and follow it as it moves, bombs are thrown to a landing point, and only the players being aimed at see a warning.
cases.technical: TargetingSystem locks on to the candidate nearest the aim point, inside a screen radius that shrinks with distance, after range, line-of-sight, visibility, and health checks. BezierProjectile flies a quadratic Bezier whose control point is recomputed every frame from the target's current position, so the arc bends to follow a moving target; the arc's offset is built from the thrower's current gravity direction rather than world up, and it flattens as the shot closes in. The Homing Projectile and the Gravity Distortion attack share this path, and an unlocked Homing Projectile travels straight with a swept raycast each frame. For other players, the power-up companion flies the same trajectory, timed from the server clock. Hostile trajectories are tagged on the server: homing shots warn only the locked target and bombs warn players near the landing point, through an indicator that tracks the projectile, pins to the screen edge when it is off-screen, and intensifies as it closes.
cases.tradeoff: Hits are detected on the thrower's client. The server checks each claimed damage hit, including a live round, range, damage bounds, a per-target cooldown, and a matching tool authorization, but does not re-simulate the flight or re-check line of sight at impact. Read directly from source in a September 2026 autosave; not re-tested in play.
claims: Editorial evidence: GD projectiles, source read 2026-09-10

cases.title: Authorizing power-ups on the server
cases.player: Bombs, gravity flips, shields, and invisibility behave normally; the checks behind them are invisible.
cases.technical: CombatAuthService treats a server-observed Tool.Activated as the root of authority, because a client cannot fire that server-side event by calling a remote. Each real activation mints short-lived grants scoped to one tool and one character instance, so they do not survive a respawn. Damage grants are payload-locked: the requested damage, stagger, and damage type must match the profile of the tool that minted them. Buffs such as invisibility and shields are applied and expired by the server. Cosmetic effect broadcasts draw on a separate budget, so visual effects cannot be spammed at other players through the effects remote.
cases.tradeoff: This limits what a modified client can trigger; it is not a complete anti-cheat. Grants are budgeted per activation with a stacking ceiling rather than tied to one specific hit. DamageHandler was read directly and consumes a matching grant before applying damage; the gravity-flip and effect handlers were identified from source comments rather than re-read line by line.

notes: Implementation verified through the supplied source audit; the current released-build traversal and procedural-course captures are pending.
Release status was supplied by the developer. No player counts or performance results are presented.
Projectile behavior was read directly from a September 8, 2026 source autosave. It has not been re-tested in play.
attribution: The surface-detection method is adapted from EmilyBendsSpace’s DevForum gravity-controller example. My work here covers integrating that method with movement, animation, and the rest of the game.

features.title: Movement and generated courses
features.description: Run along floors, walls, and ceilings through courses assembled from connected rooms.

features.title: Power-ups and abilities
features.description: Lucky Blocks along the course hand out twelve power-ups, from bombs and forced gravity flips to shields, invisibility, and speed boosts. The odds shift with race position, favoring catch-up items for players at the back.
features.note: Power-up effects are authorized on the server, which limits what a modified client can trigger. It is not a complete anti-cheat.

features.title: Projectiles
features.description: Homing shots lock on to a racer near your aim, curve toward them along an arc that bends with your current gravity, and follow them as they move. Bombs are thrown to a landing point. Players being aimed at get an on-screen warning that grows more urgent as the shot closes in.
sources: Source read 2026-09-10 (September 8 autosave): Homing Projectile ProjectileController, BezierProjectile, TargetingSystem, ProjectileWarningSystem / ProjectileWarningUI, PowerUpCompanion client and server, bomb and Gravity Distortion controllers, DamageHandler
features.note: Hits are detected by the thrower’s game and then checked by the server, which does not re-simulate the flight.

features.title: Currencies, shop, and cosmetics
features.description: A coins-and-keys economy connects the shop, rotating cosmetic crates, and player inventory.
features.note: The crate shop screenshot uses the owner test account’s balances. It shows the shop, not a live Robux purchase.

features.title: Saved player profiles
features.description: Cosmetic and progression changes share a saved player profile.
features.note: No save-and-return recording is shown; saving is described from the code.
